title: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
text:
November 20, 2026
Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
For release at 4:15 p.m. EST
The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail.
"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy."
This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University.
Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations.
For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

title: Federal Reserve Board releases results from survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances
text:
November 20, 2026
Federal Reserve Board releases results from survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances
For release at 10:00 a.m. EST
The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released results from a survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances. The Senior Financial Officer Survey is used by the Board to obtain information about banks' reserve balance management strategies and practices, their expectations around the size of their balance sheets and deposit balances their activity in money markets, and their views on other matters, such as operations on weekends and holidays.
The survey was conducted in collaboration with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York between September 18, 2026, and September 28, 2026, and includes responses from banks that held around three-fourths of total banking system reserve balances at the time of the survey.
For media inquiries, please e-mail [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

title: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
text:
November 20, 2026
The U.S. Economy in Global Context
At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
Watch Live
Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking.
I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently.
Geopolitics and Trade
Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated.
A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room.
The Global AI Buildout
The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world.

title: Waller, Opening Remarks
text:
November 20, 2026
Opening Remarks
Governor Christopher J. Waller
At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1
We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University.
Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy.
A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.
Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions.
Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools.
In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade.
I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose.

title: What Do Foreign Trends Tell Us About Future U.S. Labor Force Dynamics?
text:
Growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero with the recent sharp drop in net immigration. Given the ongoing decline in the native-born working-age population, the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink. The demographic path the U.S. may soon navigate has already been trod by several other advanced economies that have experienced more rapid population aging and historically lower immigration. This post lays out the basic facts about advanced economy (AE) experiences since 2014 and raises the prospect that the demographic headwinds long visible abroad may now be coming into clear view at home.
Demographic and Labor Force Trends
The table below shows percentage changes in three variables from 2014 to 2025: working-age (ages 15-64) populations, prime-age (ages 25-54) populations, and the active population, or labor force. The countries shown are the sixteen largest AEs, ordered by economic size. We also show median values for a larger set of thirty-six AEs and for developments in China, at the bottom of the table.
Level-Setting AE Population and Labor Force Growth
AE Population and Labor Force Growth Since 2014 (percent)
The first column shows wide variation in the growth of working-age populations. Growth has been negative for seven of the countries shown, with particularly marked declines in Japan, Italy, Poland, and Taiwan. Growth has also been negative in the median AE. Yet several countries have seen gains of more than 5 percent. Growth in the U.S. was solidly positive at 3 percent, but not near the top.
Variation in the growth of prime-age populations, shown in the second column, has been still more striking, ranging from dramatic declines (Japan, Germany, Italy, and Spain) to marked increases (Canada, Australia, and Sweden). Again, the U.S. stands toward the higher end of the distribution. Larger declines in the prime-age population than in the working-age population (note the gap in Spain) imply that a large share of the population has moved into the 55-64 age group and will drop out of the traditional working-age population over the coming decade. As we’ll see shortly, the variation in countries’ demographic trajectories is mostly an immigration story.
The third column of the table shows labor force growth since 2014. The contrast with demographic developments is stark. Where working-age populations have grown, active populations have grown more strongly; where working-age populations have declined, active populations have defied demographic gravity. (Indeed, in our broader sample of thirty-six AEs, only Greece and Latvia saw small labor force declines.) In several cases, the contrast can only be termed remarkable. Japan, for example, saw 6 percent labor force growth on a 7 percent drop in its working-age population. Germany saw almost 6 percent growth on a 2 percent decline in its working-age population—and a drop of more than 8 percent in the high-attachment prime-age population.
A Boost from Labor Force Participation
The gap between growth in active and working-age populations implies that labor force participation has been increasing. The table below illustrates this phenomenon across three dimensions, showing changes in participation rates among the traditional working-age population (ages 15-64), working-age women, and the “young old” (ages 65 to 74).
Rising Female and “Young Old” Participation Have Insulated AE Labor Forces
Changes in Labor Force Participation Since 2014 (percentage points)
As shown in the first column, the trend toward increased participation has been essentially universal across AEs. Gains in several countries peaked at 5 percentage points (ppt), with the median country seeing an increase of 4 ppt. Higher participation among women made an important contribution to the general increase, with the median country seeing an increase of more than 5 ppt. title: When Is Monetary Policy Transmission Strongest?
text:
Prior research shows the Federal Reserve responds more aggressively to demand-driven inflation than supply-driven inflation, consistent with its balanced approach when policy goals for employment and prices conflict. While this implies that short-term interest rates are more sensitive to demand-related conditions, recent analysis shows the same holds for longer-horizon yields. Policy surprises primarily pass through to longer-horizon forward rates during demand-driven inflationary episodes. With the recent reemergence of supply-side inflationary pressures, monetary policy surprises are likely to have a smaller impact on longer-horizon yields.
The reemergence of supply-driven inflation pressures since the pandemic has prompted a deeper examination of how the underlying sources of inflation affect monetary policy. Recent evidence indicates that whether inflation is driven by supply or demand is a key determinant of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate policy decisions (Hoffman, Manea, and Mojon 2024 and Kakhbod, Kermani, and Maciel 2026). Specifically, the Fed tends to be more aggressive in responding to demand-driven than supply-driven inflationary pressures. This asymmetry in monetary policy decisions aligns with the Fed’s 2025 Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, which discusses a “balanced approach” when employment and price stability goals conflict, as they tend to do in response to supply shocks.
While this evidence implies that short-term interest rates tend to be more sensitive to demand-driven inflationary pressures, it is not known if the same sensitivity holds true for longer-horizon yields. Financial markets may take into account the underlying reasons behind Fed policy changes, which itself depends on the source of inflationary pressure. In this Economic Letter, we assess whether the degree to which monetary policy surprises are transmitted to bond markets varies with the source of inflationary pressure at the time of the policy change.
To address this question, we use high-frequency data from the San Francisco Fed’s U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD), as developed in Acosta et al. (2026). This data set isolates policy “surprises”—the unexpected component of Fed announcements. Because these surprises are not already anticipated, tracking their immediate impact on forward rates—what the market expects interest rates to be in the future—provides a relatively clean measure of monetary policy transmission. We test whether the pass-through of these surprises into Treasury forward rates is associated with the underlying source of inflation, using the San Francisco Fed’s supply- and demand-driven inflation breakdown. Our analysis indicates that these surprises primarily pass through to longer-horizon forward rates during demand-driven inflationary episodes. That is, monetary policy transmission is strongest during episodes of demand-driven inflationary pressures. This also implies that because supply-side inflation pressures have increased in recent years, monetary policy shocks will likely have a more muted impact on longer-horizon yields.
The source of inflation pressure matters
Our analysis uses the San Franscisco Fed’s Supply- and Demand-Driven PCE Inflation data series which separates personal consumption expenditures inflation into distinct components. The series is based on methodology developed in Shapiro (2026) that identifies these drivers by assessing the joint movement of price and quantity indexes within individual categories. When prices and quantities move in the same direction, the change is attributed to demand-side factors, and when they move in opposite directions, it is attributed to supply-side factors.
Figure 1 shows the contributions of these factors to headline PCE since 2004, the beginning of the sample period used in our analysis. The supply component tends to move more with food and energy prices, while the demand component fluctuates more during recessions. T

title: Hyperscalers’ Financing of the AI Investment Boom
text:
Hyperscalers’ Financing of the AI Investment Boom
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- “Hyperscalers” — large tech firms involved in data centers and computer chips — are drawing from substantial financial resources to fund investment during the AI boom.
- Hyperscalers’ high operating profitability has provided capacity to finance greater investment with internal funds.
- Hyperscalers’ corporate debt relative to assets has fallen in recent years and remains below that of other publicly traded U.S. firms. Payments to shareholders have declined since 2022 and converged with those of other firms, suggesting hyperscalers are retaining money.
- Data center builders lean more heavily on debt and have reduced shareholder payouts to fund growing investment, while computer chip suppliers cover more-modest levels of investment with operating cash flow.
In our previous blog post, we showed that, since the beginning of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, an increase in capital expenditures and research and development (R&D) at major U.S. technology companies has corresponded with a decline in cash holdings. The decline in cash holdings, however, does not identify how these companies funded their expanding investments. Today, we will examine debt, shareholder payouts, operating income and cash holdings as possible sources of financing.
Our researchThis two-part series outlines findings from our Nov. 10, 2026, article. See Julian Kozlowski, Masataka Mori, Juan M. Sánchez and Nicholas Sullivan, “Financing Artificial Intelligence: Cash, Debt, and Corporate Investment,” Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Review, Fourth Quarter 2026, Vol. 108, No. 13, pp. 1-20. focuses on 10 large technology firms: Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., Apple Inc., Broadcom Inc., Intel Corp., International Business Machines Corp. (IBM), Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp., Nvidia Corp. and Oracle Corp. As before, we refer to this group as “hyperscalers,” using a broad definition that includes semiconductor suppliers alongside cloud and data center operators. We define the AI era as 2018 to the present, which corresponds to significant advancements in deep learning.
This analysis relies on current balance sheet and cash flow measures and does not capture off-balance-sheet commitments, such as future lease obligations, purchase obligations or remaining performance obligations, which may represent a significant share of data center builders’ forward-looking investment and financing plans.
Debt, Payouts, Profitability and Cash Holdings
Firms can obtain additional resources by increasing borrowing, retaining funds that would otherwise be distributed to shareholders, or relying on internally generated earnings and cash holdings. In the figures below, we show how these measures differ between hyperscalers and all other publicly traded U.S. firms.
The first figure reports debt-to-assets ratios from the first quarter of 2010 to the first quarter of 2026. Hyperscalers’ leverage rose substantially during the first half of the sample period, but it remained below that of other firms throughout. More recently, hyperscalers’ ratio fell from nearly 30% in 2023 to roughly 25% in early 2026. The ratio for other firms remained close to 34%. Thus, even if the dollar amount of hyperscalers’ debt has increased, it has grown more slowly than their total assets in recent years. The recent investment expansion has, therefore, not been accompanied by a comparable increase in hyperscalers’ balance sheet leverage.
Firms’ net payments to shareholders encompass dividends as well as share repurchases (net of shares issued). In the second figure, we look at net shareholder payouts scaled by firms’ total assets. Hyperscalers distributed more to shareholders than other firms did throughout most of the period. Their payout ratio reached approximately 4% in 2022 but then declined to about 2% by early 2026. title: ECB expands acceptance of DLT-based assets as eligible Eurosystem collateral
text:
- PRESS RELEASE
ECB expands acceptance of DLT-based assets as eligible Eurosystem collateral
23 November 2026
- Eurosystem to accept assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation and made available on the TARGET2-Securities platform as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations
- Decision is part of a roadmap to explore eligibility and on-chain mobilisation of assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks
- New milestone underlines Eurosystem’s commitment to innovation and fostering technological progress in European financial markets
The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) has approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This is a new milestone in the roadmap towards making the Eurosystem collateral framework fit for a tokenised European financial market ecosystem, which entails exploring ways to accept and mobilise tokenised assets in their native form.
“We support innovation without lowering our standards”, says Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel. “A future-proof collateral framework must embrace new technologies without compromising on safety or the rigour of our risk assessment.”
The decision supports the expansion of the eligibility of DLT-based assets in the Eurosystem’s collateral framework through a measured, controlled and technology-neutral approach. At the same time, it ensures that the Eurosystem’s collateral framework remains robust, adaptable, future-proof and aligned with the Eurosystem’s broader work on tokenisation and Appia objectives.
To be eligible, the assets must meet all standard collateral eligibility criteria. The arrangements for mobilising these assets must comply with applicable Eurosystem requirements. This includes making the assets available to the Eurosystem via an eligible link to a central securities depository (CSD) operating an eligible securities settlement system. In line with the existing eligibility framework for Eurosystem credit operations, the securities settlement systems must comply with the Central Securities Depositories Regulation and offer settlement in the TARGET2-Securities platform. In addition to being licensed under the DLT Pilot Regime Regulation, DLT platforms will need to meet dedicated Eurosystem requirements to ensure legal certainty and operational safety regarding, for example, settlement finality designation and the outsourcing of critical functions. The Eurosystem expects to communicate the details of these requirements in the spring of 2027, with implementation planned to take effect in June 2027.
As stated by ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone, “Pontes and Appia are helping turn Europe’s vision for tokenised finance into reality. And by adapting our collateral framework, we are further enabling the European tokenised finance market to grow, while upholding the principles of safety, efficiency and a level playing field.”
Today’s decision follows the announcement on 27 January 2026 to accept as collateral assets issued in CSDs using DLT-based services. While the Eurosystem’s roadmap foresees further exploration of ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks, today’s decision will significantly contribute to the interoperability between DLT platforms and traditional systems, thereby fostering integration in the current hybrid environment.

title: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
text:
- SPEECH
Acting in time
Keynote speech by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress
Frankfurt am Main, 20 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.
For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.
Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.
Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.
Why Europe acts in some crises but not others
It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.
Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.
Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.
Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.
What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.
Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is c

title: Made in Europe
text:
We are living through a period of radical transformation. Technological progress is accelerating alongside profound geopolitical shifts, rewriting the rules that have governed global growth, trade and security for decades.
In this polarised world, Europe is often portrayed as a continent in decline, squeezed between geopolitical rivals, held back by excessive regulation and struggling to keep pace with rapid technological change.
In my remarks this morning, I will argue that although this narrative is appealing in its simplicity, it is misleading.
By many measures, Europe is among the regions with the highest quality of life, grounded in strong institutions, a high degree of social protection and an exceptional capacity to adapt in times of crisis.
Europe can build on these fundamentals to become even stronger.
I will explain that the key is to unlock the full potential of the Single Market – one of Europe’s most powerful assets – to deliver what Europe lacks today: not talent, not ideas, not research – but scale.
A 28th regime would be a true game changer in this respect.

title: Economic activity, prices, and monetary policy in Japan
text:
I. Current Situation and Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices
Economic Activity
The Bank of Japan assesses the current situation of Japan's economy as follows: "Japan's economy has recovered moderately, although some weakness has been seen in part, partly due to the impact of the situation in the Middle East." To elaborate on this point, I would like to examine several elements of the economy, starting with developments in overseas economies.
Regarding overseas economies, uncertainties heightened considerably in spring 2026, reflecting the situation in the Middle East, but since then, real economic activity has not seen a significant downward deviation on the whole (left panel of Chart 1). Against this backdrop, the Bank assesses that "overseas economies have grown moderately on the whole, although some weakness has been seen in part." Looking at international commodity prices, crude oil prices have been at fairly high levels, as the situation in the Middle East remains unclear, but they have fallen below their peak levels reached in April (right panel of Chart 1). On the other hand, copper prices have remained elevated, partly reflecting strong global AI-related demand.
